preamble: The diphthongization of a close-mid back rounded vowel /o/ to a diphthong with a front offglide, [oɪ̯]/[ɔɪ̯]. It is documented historically in Yiddish, where Middle High German long ô became Standard (YIVO) and Polish Yiddish /ɔɪ/ (spelled ⟨וי⟩, romanized oy), while German kept /oː/ (MHG hôch > Yiddish hoykh, German hoch); Lithuanian Yiddish has [eɪ] instead, and Netherlandic Yiddish [ɔu]. A conditioned version occurs in Brazilian Portuguese, where stressed vowels of final syllables develop a [ɪ̯] offglide before a coda sibilant (arroz [aˈhoɪ̯s], pôs [ˈpoɪ̯s]).

examples.note: MHG long ō > Yiddish /ɔɪ/ (YIVO, Polish Yiddish); Lithuanian Yiddish [heɪχ].
The same long ō gives /ɔɪ/; compare German schon.
Most Brazilian speakers diphthongize a stressed vowel in a final syllable before a sibilant coda (written s or z); the glide is optional.
Same conditioned diphthongization; Rio de Janeiro [ˈpo(ɪ̯)ʃ].
